title: One Atmosphere, One Framework: How Science and AI Connect Views of Global Risk
summary: Explore how Verisk combines atmospheric science and AI to model interconnected catastrophe risks, reveal cross-peril dependencies, and inform capital decisions.
body_markdown:
*Originally published by The Insurer during the 2026 Rendez-Vous de Septembre in Monte Carlo.*


Catastrophe models subdivide the globe by borders and perils, but the atmosphere isn’t subject to human-drawn boundaries. The perils that modelers attempt to simulate occur within one connected, planetary-scale circulation that can simultaneously shape a European windstorm season, drive flood risk in Australasia, and spark severe convective activity across the United States. Yet the industry historically has modeled that worldwide system in region- and peril-specific fragments, as though each were independent. They’re not. The teleconnections and cross-peril dependencies that fragmented models can’t see are precisely what drive the tail of catastrophe risk.


Consider how a single climate state ripples across the globe. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation shifts sea-surface temperatures across the tropical Pacific, and its influence radiates outward – modulating Atlantic hurricane activity, reshaping the environment for US severe convective storms, and altering precipitation from South America to Australasia, often in the same season. These are not coincidences but a common driver. A portfolio spread across those regions and perils carries dependencies that separately built models, each blind to the others, cannot represent – and these correlations shape the tail when several perils activate together.


This is why correlation cannot be added as an afterthought or bolted onto regional models built in isolation: the correlations that matter live in the physics of the connected system, and a model that never simulated that system cannot recover them. Capturing the tail correctly means simulating the one atmosphere as one atmosphere.


## Science, scale and AI


Building it demanded an advance on three fronts: the science, the scale of data, and the AI that binds them. None replaces physics; together they reach what physics alone never could.


The science simulates the whole global circulation from first principles, conditioned on the near-present climate – the same conditioning already embedded in Verisk’s updated US severe thunderstorm and tropical cyclone models – so the baseline is today’s atmosphere, not a historical average. The scale has no precedent: a hundred thousand realizations of any given year, orders of magnitude beyond the observed record and enough to reveal the rare, multi-peril combinations history has not yet produced.


AI does what neither physics nor human effort could at this scale: correcting biases against observed reality, resolving local detail, and holding the frequency and intensity of extremes true to the record – with physics-based guardrails and validation from leading academic scientists keeping every output defensible.


For a reinsurer or carrier, none of this is academic. Diversification credit rests on the assumption that perils and regions are largely independent. Where they share an atmospheric driver, that assumption can overstate or understate diversification, distorting the true tail. Simulating the connected system corrects that: cross-peril and cross-region accumulations that were invisible become measurable; probable maximum loss and aggregate exceedance curves reflect genuine co-occurrence rather than the distortion independence introduces; and capital can be held against the world as it is.


None of this comes at the expense of local fidelity. Each peril and region is still validated against local hazard and claims experience – the global frame adds context, it does not replace the detail. The shift is from modeling a fragmented world to modeling the single system that produces it. For anyone whose capital depends on the tail, that changes what can be known.
